performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
question: What makes an interruption sound foreign to the music it interrupts?
intro: Two lyrical ideas are interrupted by an insistently repeated tune and rough orchestral responses. The return has to recover not only a melody but the manner of playing it.

sections.mNote: an oboe-led idea with uneven phrase movement

cues.title: A song with uneven steps
cues.text: The oboe’s opening line moves over a light string accompaniment. Its changing phrase lengths and shifting metre prevent the melody from becoming a square, regularly balanced march.
cues.evidence: Score p. 68, opening oboe line, alternating metres and string accompaniment: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The cached analysis confirms an active, comparatively restrained opening; metre comes from the notation, not the automatic tempo estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A rise inside the song
cues.text: The first song has its own rise and retreat before the broader contrasting melody arrives. Follow this internal swell rather than treating each change of intensity as a new theme.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-intermezzo.txt: novelty at 0:32 and 0:44; level rises from −20.0 dB at 0:35 to −11.7 at 0:45, then falls to −24.7 at 1:05. These are contour measurements, not thematic identification.

cues.title: The second song opens out
cues.text: The Calmo passage gives a broader melody to the strings, with harp chords helping to support it. Compare its longer breath with the more irregularly moving first idea.
cues.evidence: Score p. 70, Calmo from printed bar 43, viola melody and harps before the wider string statement: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 1:06 and 1:10, with a level rise at 1:10, anchors the approximate change. Bar numbers follow the historical print, whose upbeat numbering is discussed by Móricz.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ballet that never happened
cues.text: The concerto briefly had another possible future. Bartók prepared a piano reduction while a ballet version was being discussed with American Ballet Theatre; the contract was signed in January 1944, but the ballet was never performed.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments, source A-piano, describes the contract of 6 January 1944 and the unperformed ballet: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf . This is not presented as choreography for the present passage.

cues.title: A less courteous visitor
cues.text: The interruption gives a repeated tune to the clarinet and answers it with rougher orchestral gestures. The intrusion changes the manner of phrasing as much as the instrumental colour.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 72–75, printed bars 77 onward, clarinet figure, brass replies and string glissandi: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 2:10 and high onset activity around 2:15–2:20 anchor the interruption approximately. Its individual gestures are not note-synchronised.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognising the musical visitor
cues.text: The repeated tune is commonly identified with the march episode in Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony. Recognising that connection does not settle every account of Bartók’s motive, or prove one exclusive target for the joke.
cues.evidence: Rodda identifies the Shostakovich connection: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. The cue deliberately withholds the programme note’s more specific claims about satire, Hitler and Lehár as an established account of Bartók’s intention.

cues.title: A different kind of interruption
cues.text: Reviewing this performance in 1949, Douglas Watt preferred the long-playing disc because it avoided the breaks between record sides. Those physical interruptions were separate from the one Bartók deliberately wrote into the music.
cues.evidence: Douglas Watt, Concert Records, The New Yorker, 12 March 1949 issue, identifies Columbia set 793 and LP ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance and praises the LP’s lack of interruptions: https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1949/03/12/concert-records .

cues.title: The interruption does not win
cues.text: The closing music is restrained rather than triumphant. Listen to the small remaining phrases and the space around them: the lyrical manner has survived without requiring a large final statement.
cues.evidence: The report places all windows from 3:55 onward below −25 dB, reaching −34.7 at 4:25. Score pp. 77–78 supplies the closing wind fragments and quiet ending: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. No precise cadence or final-note time is asserted.

transitions.title: The phrase finds a longer breath
transitions.how: The first idea subsides and the Calmo melody opens out in the strings. Harp chords support its more sustained course. Rather than making the whole orchestra louder at once, Bartók changes the phrase’s breadth and the accompaniment’s manner.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 70, printed bar 43: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 1:06 and 1:10, with the recorded level rising after the preceding trough. The cue is aligned to a passage, not the exact viola entry.

transitions.title: The shorter phrase reappears
transitions.how: The broader song withdraws and the earlier, more lightly articulated material returns. A reduced texture and shorter gestures recover the first idea’s manner, but the return is curtailed: it will not simply repeat the opening’s full course.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 70–72, return after the Calmo span: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 1:44 and 1:48; level falls to −28.1 dB at 1:45. Approximate first-song return.

transitions.title: Repeated notes displace the song
transitions.how: A clarinet figure insists on repetition where the preceding music had allowed a flexible melodic line. Acceleration and blunt brass responses make the new episode an intrusion in behaviour as well as in tune. The interruption is composed into the movement, not a break in this transfer.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 72 onward, accelerando into the clarinet figure and brass response: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 2:02 and 2:10, followed by greater onset activity at 2:15–2:20. No transfer fault is inferred.

transitions.title: The intrusion loses its weight
transitions.how: The rough replies die away and the Calmo melody returns in a quieter string texture with harp support. The song does not defeat the interruption with an even louder response; it resumes its own way of moving.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 76, Calmo at printed bar 120: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The measured retreat to −29.4 dB at 3:00 precedes the quieter renewed line; the 3:02 boundary is an approximate passage placement.

transitions.title: The recovered song passes to winds
transitions.how: The abbreviated Calmo return gives way to the first idea again. Wind phrases now stand more exposed as the accompaniment thins. The familiar melodic manner survives, but the route back is lighter and more fragmentary than the opening.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 76–77, oboe return at printed bar 127 and subsequent wind exchanges: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. A strong quiet trough and novelty peak around 3:20 support the approximate return.

transitions.title: The phrase loosens before the close
transitions.how: The final page loosens the phrase into freer flute writing before the last short exchanges. Held accompaniment and local pauses open space around the line. The close remains small in scale; the disruptive episode is not brought back for a final flourish.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 77–78 includes rallentando, fermatas and “quasi Cadenza” before the closing a tempo: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Strong novelty at 3:40 and 3:52 locates this broader closing passage; the anchor is not the exact cadenza onset.

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, IV
source.locator: Printed pp. 68–78. Approximate passage map using the measured contrasts near 70, 104, 130, 182, 202 and 232 seconds; allow roughly 10 seconds. Historical printed bar numbers count the upbeat, as discussed in Móricz’s Comments. The map is not instrument recognition.

timeline.note: Oboe-led first song above a lightly articulated string accompaniment (p. 68).
The first idea passes among wind colours with strings below it (pp. 68–70).
Calmo: violas introduce the broad song, then violins expand it over harp harmony; cor anglais joins later in the passage (p. 70).
A reduced first-song return prepares the intrusion (pp. 71–72).
Repeated clarinet material meets brass replies, glissandi and sharply articulated orchestral gestures across the interruption (pp. 72–75).
The Calmo song returns with muted strings and harp after the intrusion (p. 76).
Wind phrases recover the first idea; strings withdraw and rejoin around the exchanges (pp. 76–77).
The quasi-cadenza flute passage unfolds over held horn and string support before the final short exchanges (p. 78).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
